cells.stance: Belief, bred by counted chances
cells.note: Probability is a felt strength of assent, but one produced mechanically by the proportion of chances or of past experiments: a psychology of frequency rather than a definition.

cells.stance: Relative to our knowledge and our ignorance
cells.note: Probability measures a state of information: two observers with different data rightly assign different probabilities to the same event.

cells.stance: Wholly in the mind — a “quantity of knowledge”
cells.note: Jevons rejects “belief” as too psychological but keeps probability mental and normative: it measures what belief ought to be, given what we know.

cells.stance: How often a kind of inference carries truth
cells.note: In 1878 Peirce defines probability as a long-run truth-ratio of an argument form, crediting Venn; belief enters only as its logarithmic “thermometer”.

cells.stance: A proportion in an endless series
cells.note: The founding statement of the frequency view: probability is the limiting proportion of a class within a series; belief is a psychological accompaniment, not the subject.

cells.stance: Both: advice to a gambler, and the long-run record
cells.note: Poincaré names subjective and objective probability side by side and makes their agreement the thing to be explained.

cells.stance: Relative to data: a logical relation
cells.note: Russell (thanking Keynes in his preface) treats probability as relative to given data, so new data change it without refuting the earlier estimate.

cells.stance: No such thing as chance
cells.note: Chance is a negative word for our ignorance of causes, yet that ignorance produces real degrees of belief.

cells.stance: Only ignorance: the vast intelligence
cells.note: The demon passage: to a sufficiently vast intellect nothing is uncertain; a molecule of vapour is as determined as a planet.

cells.stance: “Chance” is a wholly incorrect expression
cells.note: Darwin uses “chance” only to confess ignorance of the causes of variation, not to deny they exist.

cells.stance: Chance exists not in nature
cells.note: Jevons follows Laplace explicitly: chance cannot coexist with knowledge and every event was determined from the first.

cells.stance: Absolute chance: spontaneity in nature
cells.note: The 1892 Peirce breaks with determinism: law is approximate, and irregular departures are real. His 1878 essay had warned against speaking of “inherent” chance.

cells.stance: Beside the point: probability needs only ignorance
cells.note: Probability is indifferent to whether events are caused; it requires only that we cannot predict individuals and can rely on averages.

cells.stance: More than ignorance: small causes, great effects
cells.note: Poincaré states the ignorance view in order to reject it: fortuitous phenomena are those where tiny differences in causes produce large differences in effects.

cells.stance: Equal chances are “the very nature of chance”
cells.note: Hume describes, rather than defends, the mind treating each face of a die as alike probable.

cells.stance: Foundational: cases “equally possible”
cells.note: Equal possibility is defined by equal indecision, and extended to an unknown chance itself, which may be anything from zero to one.

cells.stance: Sound: treat equals equally
cells.note: Jevons defends the principle as rational even-handedness with knowledge, while conceding Boole's point that Laplace's prior is “in some degree arbitrary”.

cells.stance: Absurd: it depends on how you count
cells.note: Peirce's partition argument: re-describe the possibilities and indifference gives different answers; applied to nested regions it yields probabilities summing past one.

cells.stance: Arbitrary unless statistics decide
cells.note: Without frequencies of the causes, equal-likelihood assumptions are guesses; with them, the principle is unnecessary.

cells.stance: A convention, safe only where it washes out
cells.note: Bertrand's chord shows good sense dictating rival conventions; the calculus is trustworthy only where any continuous convention gives the same result.

cells.stance: Not a probability at all, but a “proof”
cells.note: Writing before the rule existed, Hume classes the sunrise as a proof from uniform experience, while insisting its denial is perfectly conceivable.

cells.stance: Holds: 1,826,214 to one — as a floor
cells.note: Laplace gives the rule and the famous bet, then adds that knowledge of the solar system makes the true odds incomparably greater.

cells.stance: Holds — and shows how far inference fades
cells.note: Jevons applies the rule boldly (planets, metals, pilot fish) and draws a sober moral: predictions pushed far beyond the data fall towards one half.

cells.stance: It “betrays its origin” at m = 0
cells.note: Set the observations to zero and the rule returns one half for a totally unknown event: the conceptualist principle Peirce has already rejected.

cells.stance: “Hard to take such a rule as this seriously”
cells.note: Venn traces the rule to bag-and-ball assumptions, quotes Laplace's odds and Jevons's shark, and finds no statistical confirmation that events repeat this way.

cells.stance: More cases, nearer certainty — never certainty
cells.note: Russell endorses the qualitative content of the rule as a principle of induction, while the chicken shows it can fail at the last.

cells.stance: Not by reasoning: by custom
cells.note: Any probable argument for the uniformity of nature presupposes it. Expectation rests on custom, not reason.

cells.stance: Induction is probability
cells.note: Induction and analogy are themselves probabilistic, which ties all knowledge to the calculus, though induction never establishes laws absolutely.

cells.stance: Improbable coincidence implies a cause
cells.note: Darwin uses the “doctrine of chances” as a working argument: a one-in-millions deviation recurring in a child points to inheritance.

cells.stance: Induction must rest on probability
cells.note: Jevons makes the inverse application of probability the logic of induction, and says it shows how far we outrun our data.

cells.stance: Justified as a method, in the long run
cells.note: Synthetic inference has no probability of its own; what we know is the trustworthiness of the procedure, guaranteed in the long run of inquiry.

cells.stance: Probability presupposes induction
cells.note: Every probability rests on an inductive generalisation about a series, so probability cannot ground induction; Venn names Jevons's doctrine “curious”.

cells.stance: Indispensable: science stands or falls with it
cells.note: All science is an unconscious application of the calculus; the only answer to Hume's doubt is “That is very improbable.”

cells.stance: Only by an unprovable principle
cells.note: Russell restates Hume's circle and accepts it: the inductive principle can be neither proved nor disproved by experience.

cells.stance: Only if its falsehood were more miraculous
cells.note: Hume's maxim, and his verdict that no testimony for a miracle has ever reached even probability.

cells.stance: The calculus confirms Hume
cells.note: Laplace derives the maxim from Bayes's rule: the more extraordinary the fact, the likelier the witness erred or lied.

cells.stance: Aside: criticism has “almost exploded” miracles
cells.note: Peirce makes no argument about testimony on this shelf; he records, in passing, that historical criticism has discredited miracles.

cells.stance: Not a probability question: first principles clash
cells.note: Miracles are not rare draws from an urn. Disputants who differ on universal causation cannot be moved by testimony rules.

cells.stance: The Academy's rule: “one madman the more”
cells.note: Poincaré applies Hume's comparison to circle-squarers, and admits the reasons are psychological rather than mathematical.

cells.stance: Constant causes prevail in the long run
cells.note: Bernoulli's theorem shows regularity without Providence, and Laplace extends it to institutions, justice and empires.

cells.stance: Stable proportions come from causes, not chance
cells.note: The regular proportions of an entangled bank are the output of the struggle for existence, not of chance.

cells.stance: The mean of many errors nears the truth
cells.note: For measurement, the long-run behaviour of means is the only guide when instruments disagree.

cells.stance: It defines probability — no life is long enough
cells.note: The long run is what probability means, yet every finite gambler is ruined and every life ends: the theorem points beyond the individual.

cells.stance: A “relic of Realism”
cells.note: Venn accepts long-run frequency but denies there is any objective probability for it to converge to, and warns that social series change type.

cells.stance: Real: insurance dividends are not ignorance
cells.note: The law of great numbers produces dividends that would survive an all-knowing physician: the regularity is objective.

cells.stance: Custom guides; the wise proportion belief
cells.note: Without the habit of expecting the past to repeat there would be no action at all.

cells.stance: “No arbitrariness in the choice”
cells.note: Probability is common sense reduced to calculus and can always determine the most advantageous choice.

cells.stance: Only where contradiction stays free
cells.note: Mill voices the “assurance sufficient for human life” argument as an objection, then answers it: we may act on an opinion only if it remains open to refutation.

cells.stance: “The very guide of life”
cells.note: Jevons adopts Butler's maxim and defines rational expectation as what leads, in the long run, to the least disappointment.

cells.stance: Only for an unlimited community
cells.note: Since a single case has no probability, acting on chances is rational only for someone whose interests extend to the indefinite community.

cells.stance: Through aggregates, not prophecy
cells.note: Probability cannot remove individual uncertainty but lets us act (insurance) so that its consequences matter less; beyond series it offers only rough belief.

cells.stance: It works — and acting is not the explanation
cells.note: He states the “act as if” defence and finds it too thin: insurance dividends are objective and need explaining.

cells.stance: All conduct rests on it — on an unproved principle
cells.note: Most of what passes for knowledge is probable opinion, and all conduct depends on the inductive principle.

pairs.laplace|venn: The cleanest crux on the shelf. Laplace's probability is a state of knowledge, so ignorance can be divided evenly; Venn's is a proportion in a series, so ignorance yields nothing. Their quarrels over the sunrise and the long run follow from that.
pairs.hume|laplace: Hume describes how belief follows counted chances; Laplace turns that psychology into a calculus. They agree on chance and on miracles, and part on whether induction is reasoning (Laplace) or custom (Hume).
pairs.jevons|venn: Contemporaries in open dispute: Venn calls Jevons's grounding of induction in probability “curious” and mocks the pilot-fish odds. The root is Q1: knowledge in the mind against frequency in a series.
pairs.peirce|venn: Allies on the definition (Peirce credits Venn), divided on what follows from it: Peirce makes frequency a theory of inference whose validity lives in the long run of an unlimited community, and later gives chance a place in nature.
pairs.laplace|peirce: Peirce attacks the inverse method at its root (equal probability for the unknown) and later rejects Laplace's determinism outright. Two cruxes, one logical (Q3) and one metaphysical (Q2).
pairs.laplace|poincare: Poincaré keeps Laplace's calculus but not its foundations: indifference becomes a convention that must wash out, and chance becomes instability rather than ignorance.
pairs.hume|russell: Russell restates Hume's problem in probabilistic language and accepts its force. Where Hume rests on custom, Russell rests on an inductive principle accepted for its intrinsic evidence.
pairs.jevons|peirce: Both are logicians of science. Jevons grounds induction in inverse probability; Peirce denies that synthetic conclusions have probabilities at all, only methods with track records.
pairs.poincare|venn: Both doubt the classical priors, but Poincaré takes the law of large numbers to be about the world (dividends), and Venn takes it to be about the series we construct.
pairs.hume|venn: Venn quotes Hume with approval on chance and on miracles, then argues that the miracle debate is not one that testimony rules can settle.
pairs.darwin|peirce: Darwin's “chance” confesses ignorance of the causes of variation; Peirce's 1892 cosmology makes chance a real source of variety, partly inspired by evolution.
